stem: What is a **polymer**?

options.content: a mixture of many small molecules held together by weak forces
options.rationale: A polymer is a single, very long molecule with covalent bonds along the chain, not a mixture.

options.content: a small molecule with a C=C double bond that can join to others
options.rationale: This describes an alkene monomer, not the polymer made from it.

options.content: a large molecule built up from many smaller molecules called monomers
options.rationale: This is the definition.

options.content: a giant lattice of metal ions held together by metallic bonding
options.rationale: That describes a metal; polymers are covalent molecules.

explanation: A polymer is a very large molecule (macromolecule) made by joining many small molecules, called monomers, together.

stem: Which monomer is used to make poly(ethene)?

options.content: ethane
options.rationale: Ethane is saturated and cannot polymerise.

options.content: ethanol
options.rationale: Ethanol is an alcohol, not an alkene.

options.content: propene
options.rationale: Propene makes poly(propene).

options.content: ethene
options.rationale: Its C=C double bond lets the molecules link up.

explanation: Poly(ethene) is made by addition polymerisation of ethene, CH₂=CH₂.

stem: Why can ethene form an addition polymer but ethane cannot?

options.content: Ethene has a C=C double bond that can open to link to other molecules.
options.rationale: Unsaturated molecules can add to each other.

options.content: Ethene molecules are larger, so they can reach and join their neighbours.
options.rationale: Ethene (Mᵣ 28) is slightly smaller than ethane (Mᵣ 30); size is not the reason.

options.content: Ethene is a liquid at room temperature, so its molecules can mix and join.
options.rationale: Both ethene and ethane are gases at room temperature.

options.content: Ethane's molecules are polar, so they repel each other and cannot join.
options.rationale: Ethane is a non-polar hydrocarbon; it cannot polymerise because it has no C=C bond.

explanation: Addition polymerisation needs a C=C double bond. In ethene the double bond opens and each molecule bonds to two neighbours. Ethane is saturated, so it has no double bond to open.

stem: True or false: poly(ethene) carrier bags are broken down quickly by microorganisms in the soil.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: It is false. Poly(ethene) is non-biodegradable: microorganisms cannot break it down, so it lasts for many years.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: poly(ethene) is non-biodegradable and can last for hundreds of years.

explanation: Microorganisms cannot break the long carbon chains of poly(ethene), so it is non-biodegradable. Discarded bags stay in the environment and landfill sites for a very long time.

stem: Name the type of polymerisation in which monomers with a C=C double bond join to form a polymer as the only product.

rejected.feedback: Condensation polymerisation also forms a small molecule such as water.
Condensation polymerisation also forms a small molecule such as water.

explanation: This is addition polymerisation: the C=C bonds open and the monomers join with nothing else being formed.

stem:
Which is the repeat unit of poly(propene), made from propene, $\ce{CH2=CHCH3}$?

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content; ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4.*

options.content: $\ce{-[CH2-CH2-CH2]\bond{-}}$
options.rationale: The CH₃ group does not join the main chain; it becomes a branch.

options.content: $\ce{-[CH=CH(CH3)]\bond{-}}$
options.rationale: The double bond must become a single bond in the polymer.

options.content: $\ce{-[CH2-CH2]\bond{-}}$
options.rationale: This is the repeat unit of poly(ethene); a carbon atom is missing.

options.content: $\ce{-[CH2-CH(CH3)]\bond{-}}$
options.rationale: Two chain carbons from the C=C, with CH₃ as a branch.

explanation: Only the two carbons of the double bond form the main chain. The –CH₃ group becomes a branch on every other carbon: –[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]–.
hints: Change C=C to C–C and keep every other group attached to the same carbon.

stem:
Which monomer is used to make the polymer $\ce{-[CH2-CHCl]_{n}\bond{-}}$?

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content; ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4.*

options.content: chloroethene, $\ce{CH2=CHCl}$
options.rationale: Put the double bond back between the two chain carbons.

options.content: chloroethane, $\ce{CH3CH2Cl}$
options.rationale: Chloroethane has no double bond, so it cannot form an addition polymer.

options.content: ethene and chlorine
options.rationale: The chlorine is already part of the monomer.

options.content: 1,2-dichloroethene, $\ce{CHCl=CHCl}$
options.rationale: The repeat unit has only one Cl atom.

explanation: The repeat unit –CH₂–CHCl– comes from a monomer with a C=C between these two carbons: CH₂=CHCl, chloroethene. The polymer is poly(chloroethene), PVC.
hints: Remove the outside bonds and put a C=C between the two carbons.

stem: Complete the sentences about poly(ethene).

payload.template: Poly(ethene) is made by {{blank:a}} polymerisation. The monomer is {{blank:b}}. In the polymer, each C=C double bond has become a {{blank:c}} bond.

explanation: Ethene monomers join by addition polymerisation; each C=C opens to a C–C single bond and forms new bonds to the neighbouring units.

stem: Match each polymer with a typical use.

right.content: water pipes and electrical cable insulation
drinking glasses that can be heated in a flame

explanation: Poly(ethene): bags and tanks; poly(propene): ropes, sacks and crates; PVC: pipes and insulation; PTFE: non-stick coatings. No plastic is suitable for glasses heated in a flame.
hints: PTFE is very slippery and heat-resistant.

stem: A molecule of PVC is made from 2400 molecules of chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl. Calculate the relative molecular mass of the PVC molecule. (Aᵣ: H = 1, C = 12, Cl = 35.5)
explanation: Mᵣ(CH₂=CHCl) = 24 + 3 + 35.5 = 62.5. No atoms are lost in addition polymerisation, so Mᵣ(polymer) = 2400 × 62.5 = 150 000.

stem: After heavy rain in a town, plastic bags and bottles are found blocking storm drains, and some goats are seen chewing plastic bags at the rubbish dump. Some residents burn their plastic rubbish.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why the plastic bags remain in the environment for many years.

points.description: They are non-biodegradable: microorganisms cannot break them down

parts.explanation: Plastics such as poly(ethene) are non-biodegradable: bacteria and fungi cannot break their long chains down.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe **two** problems caused by plastic litter.

points.description: Animals (livestock, wildlife) eat it or are trapped by it and may die
Builds up in rivers, lakes and oceans, harming aquatic life
Looks unsightly / breeds mosquitoes where water collects in containers

parts.explanation: Plastic litter blocks drains so that water floods streets, and animals such as goats and cattle eat bags, which can block their stomachs and kill them.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Why is burning PVC rubbish especially harmful?

options.content: It releases oxygen, which makes the fire spread quickly.
options.rationale: Burning uses oxygen; it does not release it.

options.content: It releases hydrogen chloride, a toxic and acidic gas.
options.rationale: PVC contains chlorine.

options.content: It gives only carbon dioxide and water, so it is no worse than wood.
options.rationale: PVC contains chlorine, so burning it also gives hydrogen chloride, as well as soot and carbon monoxide.

options.content: It releases ammonia, which smells and damages the lungs.
options.rationale: PVC contains no nitrogen, so it cannot form ammonia.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** ways the town could reduce the amount of plastic waste.

points.description: Reduce: encourage reusable shopping bags / charge for or ban thin plastic bags
Collect and recycle plastics (sorted by type)
Use biodegradable alternatives such as paper or cloth bags

parts.explanation: Encourage people to use reusable cloth bags instead of plastic bags, and set up collection points so that bottles and other plastics can be recycled.

explanation: Plastics are non-biodegradable, so litter persists: it blocks drains and causes flooding, harms animals and builds up in water. Burning PVC releases toxic hydrogen chloride as well as other harmful gases. Reducing, reusing and recycling plastics, and using biodegradable alternatives, cut the waste.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Non-biodegradable.
2. (b) Flooding from blocked drains; animals harmed.
3. (c) PVC → HCl when burnt.
4. (d) Reduce, reuse, recycle; biodegradable alternatives.
hints: Which element in PVC is not present in poly(ethene)?

stem:
A section of an addition polymer chain is shown:

$\ce{-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)\bond{-}}$

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content; ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4.*

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many monomer molecules were used to make the section shown?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What is the repeat unit of the polymer (the part of the chain made from one monomer molecule)?

options.content: $\ce{-[CH(CH3)]\bond{-}}$
options.rationale: This is only half of what one monomer adds: the repeat unit of an addition polymer contains both carbons of the C=C.

options.content: $\ce{-[CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)]\bond{-}}$
options.rationale: Each monomer contributes two chain carbons.

options.content: $\ce{-[CH2-CH(CH3)]\bond{-}}$
options.rationale: This is the repeat unit of poly(propene); here both carbons carry a CH₃.

options.content: $\ce{-[CH(CH3)=CH(CH3)]\bond{-}}$
options.rationale: The polymer has no C=C bonds.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Write the structural formula of the monomer.

rejected.feedback: The double bond must be between the two carbons that each carry a CH₃ group: but-2-ene.
Give the position of the double bond: but-2-ene.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain how the section shows that the polymer was made by addition, not condensation.

points.description: The chain contains only the atoms of the monomer (C and H, no linkage such as ester/amide) / no small molecule was lost, and the chain is all C–C bonds

parts.explanation: The chain is made only of the monomer's carbon and hydrogen atoms joined by C–C bonds: no atoms were lost as a small molecule, so it is an addition polymer.

explanation: The repeating section is –CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–, so six chain carbons came from three monomers. Putting the double bond back gives CH₃CH=CHCH₃, but-2-ene. The chain contains only the monomer's atoms, typical of addition polymerisation.
workedSolution:
1. Six chain carbons ÷ 2 per monomer = 3 monomers.
2. Repeat unit –CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–.
3. Replace C–C with C=C: CH₃CH=CHCH₃, but-2-ene.
hints: Each alkene monomer adds two carbon atoms to the main chain.

stem: A sample of poly(propene) used to make woven sacks has molecules with a relative molecular mass of 210 000. (Aᵣ: H = 1, C = 12)

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the relative molecular mass of propene, C₃H₆.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of propene molecules that joined to form one polymer molecule.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How many carbon atoms are in one polymer molecule?

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which property of poly(propene) makes it suitable for sacks?

options.content: It forms strong, tough fibres that do not rot.
options.rationale: Woven poly(propene) sacks are strong and long-lasting.

options.content: It dissolves easily in water.
options.rationale: A sack that dissolved would be useless.

options.content: It conducts electricity.
options.rationale: Poly(propene) is an insulator, and conduction is irrelevant for sacks.

options.content: It is biodegradable within a few days.
options.rationale: Poly(propene) is non-biodegradable.

explanation: Mᵣ(C₃H₆) = 36 + 6 = 42. No atoms are lost in addition polymerisation, so n = 210 000 ÷ 42 = 5000 monomers, containing 5000 × 3 = 15 000 carbon atoms. Poly(propene) forms strong fibres that do not rot, ideal for sacks.
hints: The polymer's Mᵣ is n × Mᵣ(monomer).

stem: Describe the environmental problems caused by the disposal of plastics, and explain how the properties of plastics cause these problems. [5]

points.description: Plastics are non-biodegradable (not broken down by microorganisms)
So they last for a very long time and fill up landfill sites / land is used up
Litter builds up in rivers, lakes and oceans (plastics are light/low density and are carried by wind and water)
Animals eat plastic or become trapped in it, and may die; drains are blocked, causing flooding
Burning plastics produces toxic gases (carbon monoxide, hydrogen chloride from PVC, soot) and carbon dioxide
Plastics are unreactive, so they do not decompose or corrode

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Most plastics are unreactive and non-biodegradable: microorganisms cannot break them down. Buried in landfill sites they last for hundreds of years, so the sites fill up and more land is needed. Because plastics are light and long-lasting, litter is carried by wind and water into drains, rivers, lakes and oceans, where it builds up; it blocks drains and causes flooding, and animals eat it or are trapped by it. If plastics are burned, they produce toxic gases such as carbon monoxide, hydrogen chloride (from PVC) and soot, as well as carbon dioxide.

explanation: Each problem (landfill, litter in water, harm to animals, toxic gases from burning) should be linked to a property (non-biodegradable, unreactive, light, combustible).
hints: Link each problem to a property of plastics.

stem: Which properties of poly(ethene) make it a good material for food containers?

options.content: It is biodegradable and dissolves in water.
options.rationale: Poly(ethene) is neither biodegradable nor soluble.

options.content: It conducts heat well and is magnetic.
options.rationale: Poly(ethene) is an insulator and is not magnetic.

options.content: It reacts with oxygen to keep food fresh.
options.rationale: Poly(ethene) is unreactive.

options.content: It is unreactive, waterproof and light.
options.rationale: It does not react with food, keeps moisture in and is easy to carry.

explanation: Poly(ethene) is unreactive (it does not react with the food), waterproof and light, and it can be moulded cheaply into containers, bags and film.

stem:
True or false: in addition polymerisation the polymer is the only product.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content; ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4.*

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: no small molecule is lost, so the polymer has all the atoms of the monomers.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Nothing else is made; that is why the polymer's Mᵣ is exactly n × Mᵣ of the monomer.

explanation: In addition polymerisation the monomers simply join through their opened double bonds. No small molecule such as water is lost, so the polymer is the only product.

stem:
Which statement about the repeat unit of an addition polymer is correct?

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content; ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4.*

options.content: It has the monomer's atoms minus one water molecule lost as it joins.
options.rationale: Losing water happens in condensation polymerisation.

options.content: It has the same atoms as the monomer, but the C=C has become a C–C bond.
options.rationale: The atoms are unchanged; only the bonding changes.

options.content: It has the same atoms as the monomer and still contains the C=C bond.
options.rationale: The double bond is used up in forming the chain.

options.content: It is always –CH₂–CH₂–, whatever alkene the polymer is made from.
options.rationale: This is true only for poly(ethene).

explanation: Addition polymerisation keeps all the atoms of the monomer. In the repeat unit the C=C has become C–C, and the two extra bonds link the unit to its neighbours.
hints: Are any atoms lost when an addition polymer forms?

stem: Why are discarded plastic bags and bottles easily carried long distances by rivers and floods?

options.content: They dissolve in the water and move with it.
options.rationale: Plastics do not dissolve in water.

options.content: They are biodegradable, so they break into small pieces quickly.
options.rationale: Most plastics are non-biodegradable.

options.content: They are light (low density) and do not break down.
options.rationale: They float and stay intact for years.

options.content: They are denser than water.
options.rationale: Most bags and bottles float.

explanation: Many plastics are less dense than water and are non-biodegradable, so they float and are carried far by rivers and floods, ending up in lakes and the sea.

stem:
PVC is the addition polymer of chloroethene, $\ce{CH2=CHCl}$. When PVC burns, all of its chlorine can be released as hydrogen chloride, HCl. (Aᵣ: H = 1, C = 12, Cl = 35.5)

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content; ZIMSEC O-Level Form 4.*

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the relative formula mass of the repeat unit of PVC.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of chlorine in PVC.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of hydrogen chloride that could be released by burning 1.0 kg of PVC, in grams.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why the hydrogen chloride released is harmful.

points.description: It is toxic / irritates the lungs and eyes, and it is acidic: it dissolves in water to form hydrochloric acid (acid rain, damage to buildings and plants)

parts.explanation: Hydrogen chloride is a toxic, choking gas that irritates the eyes and lungs; it dissolves in rain to form hydrochloric acid, which damages plants and buildings.

explanation: The repeat unit –CH₂–CHCl– has the same atoms as chloroethene: Mᵣ 62.5, of which 35.5 is chlorine (56.8%). 1.0 kg = 1000 g contains 1000 ÷ 62.5 = 16 mol of repeat units, so up to 16 mol of HCl (16 × 36.5 = 584 g) can be released.
hints: The repeat unit contains exactly the atoms of one chloroethene molecule.

stem: From which raw material are most plastics made?

options.content: limestone
options.rationale: Limestone is used for cement and lime.

options.content: sand
options.rationale: Sand is used to make glass.

options.content: crude oil
options.rationale: Cracking crude-oil fractions gives the alkene monomers.

options.content: iron ore
options.rationale: Iron ore is used to make iron and steel.

explanation: Most plastics are made from alkenes such as ethene and propene, which come from cracking fractions of crude oil.
